title: Revisions to Establish the Sixth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR 6) for Public Water Systems
pass_4_primary_concern: The main concern is whether the laboratory-capacity and cost assumptions are strong enough to support the nationwide monitoring scope.
pass_5_high_stakes_domain_reason: The rule governs drinking-water occurrence data for public water systems and can shape later contaminant decisions and compliance burdens.
pass_5_concise_why: The proposal is coherent, but the visible record is thinner than ideal on the evidence-to-burden match and the implementation assumptions behind laboratory capacity.
pass_5_most_important_consequence: If laboratory capacity or the small-system fallback fails, the rule can lose the national data it is supposed to generate while still imposing reporting and sampling obligations.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: EPA is using the SDWA/UCMR framework for a drinking-water monitoring program, so the authority fit looks ordinary.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate authority-substitution comment needed on the visible record.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The rule does not turn a side condition into the main source of power.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate statutory-inversion issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The notice keeps responsibility with EPA, states, systems, and labs in their usual roles.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate accountability-inversion issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The rule uses approved laboratories and reporting obligations, but not an obvious self-policing swap that would be structurally out of place.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate self-policing issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The AWIA scope conditions are part of the statutory design, not an obviously inverted sequence.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Only press this if the fallback sample logic becomes more restrictive than the statute appears to require.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: A nationwide 30-contaminant monitoring program is significant, and the visible record shows the rationale in summary form rather than with the full comparative record that would let commenters test the size of the intrusion against the evidence base.

evidence.quote_or_absence: The proposed UCMR 6 would require public water systems to collect national occurrence data for 30 unregulated contaminants.

pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask EPA to explain why this is the right monitoring burden for the information gap it is trying to close.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The monitoring remedy generally matches the information-collection rationale, but commenters can still ask for a tighter explanation of the path from data to later action.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask EPA to show the direct line from the new monitoring data to later SDWA decisions.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The rollout depends on lab capacity and appropriations assumptions that may be reasonable, but are not fully stress-tested in the visible notice text.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask EPA to publish the throughput and contingency assumptions behind the rollout.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The rule depends on a multi-step lab approval and reporting pipeline working smoothly across systems and states.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Ask EPA to explain the failure-handling path between approval, sampling, and reporting.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The target problem is clear: EPA wants national occurrence data for contaminants that are not yet under NPDWRs.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate threat-ambiguity issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The notice acknowledges burden, cost, and public-comment issues rather than denying them.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate impact-denial issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The program is not organized around discretionary targeting of individual entities.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate targetability issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The rule includes laboratory approval, proficiency testing, reporting, and public-database mechanisms.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate safeguard-absence issue stands out on the visible record.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The notice does not obviously shift an unbounded cleanup burden onto outsiders.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate externality-dumping issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The rule is a monitoring program, not a suspicion or flagging regime.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate suspicion-machine issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The rule improves traceability by making the collected data publicly available.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate accountability-substrate issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The rule is a monitoring action, not an irreversible control action that precludes review.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate harm-before-review issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The lab-approval and reporting steps are ordinary administrative gates rather than a novel choke point.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate gateway-control issue stands out unless capacity constraints worsen.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The consequence class is straightforward: monitoring and data publication now, possible later SDWA action.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate consequence-class ambiguity issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The notice uses ordinary monitoring standards rather than vague exclusion criteria.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: No separate ambiguity-enabled gatekeeping issue stands out.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The proposal is coherent overall, but it still depends on a visible record that is thinner than ideal on the evidence-to-burden match and implementation assumptions.
pass_5_flaws.comment_leverage: Use this as the overall framing: coherent rule, but not fully transparent record.
